title: The agent-ready web: Simplify user actions with WebMCP — Tara Agyemang, Google

summary: Tara Agyemang, a developer relations engineer on the Google Chrome team working alongside DeepMind, introduces Web MCP (Web Model Context Protocol), a proposed web standard for exposing website capabilities as structured tools to in-browser AI agents. She frames the problem: for decades the web was built for human eyes and actions, but agents now use it on humans' behalf. To buy two concert tickets, an agent might parse the entire DOM, inspect the accessibility tree, take a screenshot, compute pixel coordinates, and click—only to miss because a late-loading ad shifted the layout. The process is long, brittle, and token-heavy. Before adopting WebMCP, she stresses improving web foundations: semantic HTML, robust accessibility standards, fast page performance (core web vitals), and good UX flows make a site agent-ready by default. WebMCP is described as the USB-C of AI agent interactions—instead of agents guessing what a site does, the site offers a menu of named, typed, described actions. She demos a maze escape game navigable only via AI tool calls using a Chrome DevRel inspector extension, then demos a concert ticket purchase completed in three tool calls (search concerts by name, open concert page by ID, purchase with quantity and section) using Gemini 3.1, emphasizing that UI must stay in sync with tool calls and that checkout should remain manual so users control real spending. WebMCP differs from MCP: MCP connects agents to server-side applications, while WebMCP is client-side and browser-bound, implementing only the tools part. Two implementation APIs exist: the declarative API adds HTML attributes to forms for automatic JSON schema generation, and the imperative API uses a registerTool function with an execute block running normal JavaScript—wrapping existing functions, manipulating the DOM, and returning state to the agent. The imperative API is expected to be most used due to complex UI flows. WebMCP is in early preview on Chrome 146+, still experimental and subject to change. Setup requires Chrome Canary (recommended), enabling a testing flag, and installing the Model Context Tool Inspector extension. Resources include a blog post with early preview program sign-up for documentation and best practices, and a GitHub repository with demo code (six to seven demos including the maze), the inspector tool, and an eval CLI for testing your own sites. She calls for community feedback on friction points and bugs to iterate the API toward broader availability, concluding that WebMCP turns every website into a high-performance API for agents while building great user experiences.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker introduction
sections.summary: Tara Agyemang introduces herself as a developer relations engineer on the Google Chrome team, working with DeepMind, and invites attendees to discuss web and AI at the DeepMind booth.

sections.title: Problem: agents using the human-built web
sections.summary: The web was built for human eyes and actions, but agents increasingly use it on humans' behalf. To buy concert tickets, an agent may parse the entire DOM, the accessibility tree, take a screenshot, compute pixel coordinates, and click—only to miss because a late-loading ad shifted the layout, making the process long, brittle, and token-heavy.

sections.title: Improve web foundations first
sections.summary: Before WebMCP, improve web foundations: semantic HTML, robust accessibility standards, fast page performance (core web vitals), and good UX flows. Making a site accessible for everyone makes it accessible to AI agents by default.

sections.title: WebMCP as the USB-C of AI agent interactions
sections.summary: Web MCP is a proposed web standard that defines site capabilities as structured tools for AI agents, giving them a menu of named, typed, described actions instead of guessing.

sections.title: Maze escape game demo
sections.summary: Demo of a maze escape game built by Chrome DevRel that can only be used via AI tooling. The model context tool inspector extension lists tools; the start page has one tool, the game page has navigation tools. Gemini 1.5 maps natural-language prompts to the move tool.

sections.title: Model context tool inspector extension
sections.summary: The model context tool inspector is a Chrome DevRel extension available in the Chrome Web Store that lists tools on a page and lets users prompt or call tools directly.

sections.title: WebMCP vs MCP
sections.summary: MCP connects AI agents to server-side applications via a separate service; WebMCP is inspired by MCP and implements only the tools part, client-side, requiring an open browser window.

sections.title: Use cases
sections.summary: Use cases include booking flights, filtering products, filling complex medical or financial forms, triggering hidden page fixes, and shopping with specific filters.

sections.title: Declarative and imperative APIs
sections.summary: The declarative API adds tool name and tool description attributes to HTML forms for automatic JSON schema generation. The imperative API uses a registerTool function where developers manually define schemas for complex multi-step flows.

sections.title: Execute block details and imperative API prevalence
sections.summary: The imperative API's execute block runs normal JavaScript—developers can call existing functions, validate and trim input, create DOM elements, and return state to the agent for its next steps. The imperative API is expected to be the most used because people have more complex UI flows.

sections.title: Concert ticket purchase demo
sections.summary: Using Gemini 3.1, the demo buys two VIP tickets to the Summer Vibes Festival in three tool calls: search concerts by name (returns concert ID), open concert page by ID (exposes new tools), and purchase ticket with quantity and section. UI stays in sync with tool calls; checkout would remain manual in real life so users control spending. Total spent: £356.

sections.title: WebMCP status and setup
sections.summary: WebMCP is in early preview, very experimental, and subject to change. Setup requires Chrome 146+ (Chrome Canary recommended), enabling the WebMCP testing flag via URL, and installing the Model Context Tool Inspector extension from the Chrome Web Store for debugging.

sections.title: Resources, feedback call, and wrap-up
sections.summary: Two key resources: a blog post for the early preview program providing documentation, best practices, and implementation details upon sign-up, and a GitHub repository with the inspector tool, six to seven demos including the maze, and an eval CLI for testing your own sites. Agyemang requests community feedback on friction and bugs, and concludes that WebMCP turns every website into a high-performance API for agents while building great user experiences, urging attendees to make their sites agent-ready.
